content:
Waking up at night to pee (nocturia) becomes more common with age, and arthritis makes each trip harder. Stiff hips, knees or feet slow you down, so a sudden urge can turn into rushing, a leak or a fall. Getting up more often can also have a treatable cause. Common causes include drinking late in the evening, caffeine or alcohol, the timing of water tablets, ankle swelling that drains back into the blood when you lie down, an overactive bladder, an enlarged prostate, a urine infection, diabetes and poor sleep. Things you can try include having your last drink earlier in the evening while still drinking enough through the day, cutting down on evening tea, coffee and alcohol, raising swollen legs in the afternoon, and keeping a bladder diary for a few days to show your GP. Pelvic floor exercises and bladder training help many people, and the NHS continence service can assess you. See a GP if night trips are new, getting worse, causing leaks or falls, or come with blood in your pee or pain. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about the bladder side of night-time trips: why they happen and what can reduce them. To make the route itself safer, see night lights and safer night-time trips. If a bedside option would help, see commodes at night. For help getting on and off the toilet, see toilet frames and raised seats.

Why night trips are harder with arthritis

When you lie still for hours, joints stiffen, so the first steps out of bed are slow. If your bladder gives you little warning, there may not be time to get there comfortably. That is when people rush in the dark, skip their walking aid or try to stand too quickly, and when falls and leaks happen. Broken sleep also makes pain and tiredness worse the next day.

So reducing how often you need to go, and how urgent it feels, is as much about protecting your joints and safety as it is about the bladder.

Common reasons for waking to pee

Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust describes several common causes:

  • Age-related hormone changes: the body makes less of the hormone that slows urine production overnight, so more urine is made at night.
  • Prostate enlargement: in men, an enlarged prostate can stop the bladder emptying fully, so you need to go more often.
  • Overactive bladder: a sudden, strong need to go, sometimes with leaks before you reach the toilet.
  • Urine infections: dark, cloudy or smelly pee, burning or pain when peeing, or feeling you cannot empty your bladder. In older people an infection can also cause sudden confusion. See UTI and sudden confusion.
  • Heart problems and ankle swelling: fluid that collects in the legs during the day goes back into the blood when you lie down, and the kidneys then make more urine.
  • Diabetes: high blood sugar can make you thirsty and irritate the bladder.
  • Poor sleep: if you wake for another reason, such as pain, you are more likely to notice the urge to go. Loud snoring with pauses in breathing can be a sign of sleep apnoea, which is worth raising with a GP.
  • Drinks and medicines: large drinks near bedtime, caffeine and alcohol. Some medicines, such as water tablets, increase urine on purpose.

Things you can try

  • Move your last drink earlier: for example, have your last drink a couple of hours before bed rather than just before. Do not cut your total fluids. Guy's and St Thomas' advises still drinking about 6 to 8 cups of fluid a day, and the NHS notes that drinking too much or too little can make bladder symptoms worse.
  • Cut down on caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening: tea, coffee, cola and chocolate contain caffeine. The NHS notes that caffeine can increase the amount of urine your body makes.
  • If your ankles swell: sit or lie with your legs raised, at or above the level of your heart, for about an hour in the afternoon, as the Guy's and St Thomas' leaflet suggests. Ask your GP about support stockings and about why your ankles swell.
  • Go before bed: empty your bladder as part of your bedtime routine.
  • Keep your bowels regular: constipation can press on the bladder. Some painkillers cause constipation, so ask a pharmacist if this has started. See NHS advice on constipation.
  • Reduce long daytime naps if they are stopping you sleeping deeply at night.
  • Keep a bladder diary: for three days or so, note what and when you drink, when you pee and any leaks. The NHS says a GP may ask you to keep one, and it makes the appointment much more useful.

Medicines: ask, do not guess

Water tablets (diuretics) and some other medicines can increase night-time trips. Sometimes the timing can be changed, for example taking a water tablet earlier in the day. Only do this if your GP or pharmacist says it is right for you. Do not stop or change any prescribed medicine yourself. A pharmacist medication review is a good way to look at everything you take, including sleeping tablets, which can make night trips riskier. See sleeping tablets and night falls.

Pelvic floor exercises, bladder training and the NHS continence service

The NHS says treatments that do not involve medicines or surgery are tried first. These are lifestyle changes, pelvic floor muscle training and bladder training.

  • Pelvic floor muscle training strengthens the muscles that control the flow of urine. The NHS describes a programme that usually lasts at least 3 months, and it is best set up by a specialist who can check you are squeezing the right muscles. Many of the exercises can be done sitting down, which suits stiff hips and knees.
  • Bladder training helps with urgency by gradually increasing the time between feeling the need to go and going. The NHS says a course usually lasts at least 6 weeks.
  • NHS continence services are staffed by specialist nurses (continence advisers) and specialist physiotherapists who can assess and treat you. A GP can refer you, and in some areas you can refer yourself.
  • Products such as pads, pants or a handheld urinal do not treat the problem. They can make nights safer and less worrying while you are being assessed. Ask the continence service what is available on the NHS.

NICE has guidance for urinary incontinence in women (NG123) and for urinary symptoms in men (CG97). If these steps do not help enough, your GP or specialist can talk you through other treatments.

Make the trip shorter and safer

  • Keep your walking aid by the bed, and sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before you stand.
  • Light the route. See night lights and safer night-time trips.
  • Wear night clothes that are easy to undo with sore hands, such as elastic waists rather than buttons.
  • A commode or urinal by the bed can help during a flare or after an illness. See commodes at night.
  • An occupational therapist can suggest equipment such as toilet frames or raised seats. Ask your GP or local council for a needs assessment.

When to see a GP

  • Night trips are new, happening more often or disturbing your sleep a lot.
  • You are leaking urine or have nearly fallen, or have fallen, on the way to the toilet.
  • Your stream is weak, you strain, or you feel your bladder does not empty. Men in particular should mention this.
  • You are very thirsty, or have swollen ankles or breathlessness.

It is a common problem and GPs are used to talking about it. Treatment often helps.

When it is urgent

  • Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you see blood in your pee (pink, red or brown), have pain when peeing, or cannot pee at all.
  • Get help quickly if you have a high temperature, shivering, pain in your back or side, or new confusion, as these can be signs of a more serious infection. See UTI and sudden confusion.
  • Call 999 if someone is very unwell, cannot be woken properly or has hurt themselves badly in a fall.

For family and carers

Night trips are easy to underestimate because they happen while everyone else is asleep. Ask gently how often the person gets up at night and whether they have had any near misses. Help them keep a bladder diary, and go with them to the GP if they would like you to. Embarrassment stops many people from asking for help, so treat it as an ordinary health problem.

Common questions

Should I stop drinking in the evening?

Have your last drink a little earlier, but do not cut down on fluids overall. Drinking too little can make bladder symptoms and constipation worse.

Is getting up at night just part of getting older?

It does become more common with age. But getting up more and more often may have a cause that can be treated, so it is worth mentioning to your GP.

Can I do pelvic floor exercises if I have arthritis?

Usually yes. Many can be done sitting or lying down. A continence nurse or specialist physiotherapist can check your technique and set a programme.
